Kalau tidak silap saya, filem itu berjalan seperti biasa tetapi di pertengahan cerita sesuatu telah berlaku. Tiba-tiba budak perempuan yang menjadi pelakon utamanya merajuk. Dia tidak mahu berlakon lagi.

Saya ingat tentang itu sebab ia pelik. Kisah pelakon merajuk di set penggambaran bukan perkara asing. Ada yang bergaduh dengan pengarah, tidak puas hati dengan perubahan skrip atau berkelahi sesama pelakon atau kru. Tetapi biasanya semua itu berlaku di belakang kamera. Yang ini berlaku dalam filem.

Saya pun bertanya kepada Joe, khadam belaan saya (ChatGPT), ada tak filem luar negara yang ceritanya sedang berjalan tiba-tiba pelakonnya merajuk dan enggan meneruskan lakonan? Beberapa filem disebut tetapi tak tepat. Saya kemudiannya menyebut bahawa ia filem Iran. Tup! Rupa-rupanya memang ada. Joe berjaya mengesannya.

Filem itu The Mirror atau Ayneh, arahan Jafar Panahi yang diterbitkan pada 1997. Seperti kebanyakan filem Iran, ceritanya ringkas sahaja. Ayneh mengisahkan seorang budak perempuan bernama Mina menunggu ibunya datang mengambilnya selepas waktu sekolah. Ibunya tidak muncul. Mina akhirnya mengambil keputusan untuk pulang sendiri.

Plotnya membawa kita mengekori perjalanan budak kecil itu meredah kota Tehran. Dia bertanya orang, menaiki bas dan terus cuba mencari jalan pulang. Tangannya pula bersimen kerana patah. Sedang kita syok melayan, Mina tiba-tiba memandang kamera. Ada suara dari belakang kamera menegurnya supaya jangan melihat kamera. Tetapi Mina tidak peduli. Dia kata dia tidak mahu berlakon lagi.
Dia menanggalkan simen di tangannya. Oh! Rupanya tangan itu tidak patah pun. Itu cuma sebahagian daripada watak yang sedang dilakonkannya. Apahal ni? Itu yang saya ingat.

Mujur, filem tersebut ada di YouTube. Saya menontonnya semula. Kita nampak kelibat kru penggambaran dan pasukan produksi mula bercakap sesama sendiri. Kita yang sejak awal percaya pada cerita itu mula menggelabah sebab tiba-tiba ceritanya berubah.

Kita melihat, sutradara Panahi tidak menghentikan filemnya. Mina berjalan pulang. Kamera terus mengikutnya dari jauh. Mikrofon yang dipasang pada tubuhnya masih menangkap suaranya. Maka kita pula mengikuti perjalanan Mina yang kononnya bukan lagi watak dalam filem tetapi Mina yang sebenar.

Daripada sebuah filem fiksyen, The Mirror tiba-tiba seolah-olah menjadi sebuah dokumentari tentang seorang pelakon kanak-kanak yang merajuk dan meninggalkan penggambaran. Itulah yang membuat tiba-tiba saya teringat semula selepas bertahun-tahun. Cuma selepas mencari semula cerita di sebalik filem ini, barulah saya tahu satu perkara. Mina sebenarnya tidak merajuk. Sebaliknya, semua itu dirancang.

Panahi memang sengaja membuat ceritanya begitu. Menariknya, beliau memang sudah bermain dengan idea tersebut sejak awal, tetapi kemudiannya seorang kanak-kanak yang mula-mula dipilih untuk filem itu benar-benar enggan meneruskan lakonan dan terpaksa digantikan dengan Mina. Kejadian sebenar itu kemudian memantapkan idea Panahi untuk mengaburkan sempadan antara lakonan dengan realiti dalam The Mirror.Maknanya Mina sedang berlakon sebagai seorang pelakon yang tidak mahu berlakon. Pening juga ya?

Tetapi di situlah menariknya filem ini kerana ia membuka daya fikir kita yang ada ketikanya menganggap sempadan antara fiksyen dengan realiti itu jelas. Apabila menonton filem, kita tahu watak yang mati sebenarnya tidak mati. Watak yang menangis kemudiannya tenang sahaja minum kopi selepas pengarah menjerit “cut!”. Tetapi, kita terus menonton dan menikmatinya kerana tahu ia sebuah cereka. Kepercayaan kita pun hanya dalam ruang lingkup sebuah fiksyen. Selepas cerita tamat, semuanya selesai. Kita kembali ke dunia realiti.

Panahi melakukan sebaliknya. Ketika kita mula percaya, dia meruntuhkannya. Dia memunculkan kru filem dan kamera ke dalam layar. Dia memberitahu kita yang ini semua cuma filem. Barulah kita tersedar. Tapi, selepas memberitahu semuanya cuma filem, dia memperdayakan kita sekali lagi. Kita pula percaya bahagian selepasnya adalah realiti. Rupanya, masih ‘tipu’.

Itulah sebab filem tersebut dinamakan The Mirror. Mungkin cermin itu simbolnya. Cermin tidak berbuat apa-apa. Ia hanya memantulkan imej yang berada di hadapannya. Tetapi apa yang kita lihat di dalam cermin juga bukan benda itu sendiri. Ia cuma sebuah pantulan.

Begitu juga dengan ingatan. Kita selalu yakin sesuatu berlaku kerana kita mengingatinya dengan jelas. Sedangkan ingatan bukan rakaman yang tersimpan begitu sahaja dalam kepala. Ia bercampur dengan perasaan, tafsiran dan cerita yang kita bina selepas sesuatu kejadian. Ia juga penuh dengan sangka-sangkaan. Lama-kelamaan perasaan dan sangkaan mengambil tempat fakta sebenar. Kita tidak lagi mengingati apa yang benar-benar berlaku. Kita hanya mengingati sebahagian bab dalam segala hal yang berlaku.

Filem ini hanya saya jadikan contoh tentang kita, peristiwa dan ingatan. Sesuatu kejadian mungkin tidak berlaku tepat seperti yang kita sangka, atau ia memang berlaku tetapi kita pula tidak dapat mengingatinya dengan tepat. Selama lebih 20 tahun saya mengingati Mina sebagai seorang budak perempuan yang merajuk di tengah penggambaran sebuah filem Iran. Lucunya, ketika menulis ini saya masih gagal mengingati bagaimana The Mirror berakhir. Yang benar-benar berlaku dalam filem saya lupa. Yang tidak berlaku pula saya ingat.

Mungkin begitulah adat hidup. Beribu-ribu hari dalam hidup kita hilang begitu sahaja daripada kotak ingatan. Kita tidak ingat apa yang kita makan pada sekian-sekian hari, kita lupa siapa kawan kita yang bercakap tentang suatu falsafah yang bermakna. Tetapi ada beberapa hal kecil yang kekal di ingatan walaupun kita lupa hujung dan pangkalnya.

Mungkin hidup juga seperti kisah The Mirror yang digambarkan ini. Kita menjalani hidup tanpa membawa keseluruhan memori silam, kita hanya membawa beberapa babak yang entah kenapa kita pilih secara sedar dan tidak sedar, untuk tinggal bersama kita.
Nampaknya agak berat kali ini tulisan saya. Kalau faham, saya gembira. Jika tidak, harap ia tidak membelit dalam fikiran anda sepanjang hayat.

fb8a78c56a295957: I’ve been watching Malaysia make cars for more than 40 years. As an motoring writer, I test-drove the Proton Saga when it was launched in 1985, and saw it become the centre of attention.
The narrative then was that Proton marked the beginning of Malaysia’s journey towards becoming an automotive nation.

Four decades later, perhaps it is time to ask an uncomfortable question: What exactly are we trying to achieve? The question has become particularly relevant when BYD finally cleared the air over its Malaysian manufacturing plans.

The Chinese EV giant confirmed that its proposed factory in Tanjong Malim will not proceed. But BYD is not walking away from Malaysia. Managing director Jacob Ma says the company remains committed to local assembly and is already in advanced discussions with an established Malaysian assembly partner.
That is an important distinction. BYD will apparently assemble cars here. It just doesn't see the need to build another factory to do it.

Indeed, completely-knocked-down assembly, or CKD as we call it, has been part of Malaysian industrialisation since the 1960s. Toyota began assembling cars here in 1968. Volvo, Mercedes-Benz, Honda and many other international manufacturers followed, or were already part of that first wave.
Building an ecosystem

Over the following half-century, the legacy manufacturers and their Malaysian partners invested enormous sums in assembly plants, paint shops, tooling, component manufacturing, training and supplier development.
Then came Proton, and later Perodua. They created a Malaysian automotive ecosystem.

There are Malaysian engineers, technicians, toolmakers, component manufacturers, logistics companies and hundreds of vendors whose businesses grew around CKD manufacturing. That investment should not be casually discarded simply because the electric car has arrived.

In fact, BYD's latest decision may actually validate the value of what Malaysia already has. Why build another factory if there is already a competent Malaysian factory capable of assembling your cars?

The speculation naturally points towards Sime Motors' Inokom facility in Kulim, although BYD has not named its partner and we should therefore leave it at speculation for now. But Inokom illustrates the point beautifully.

The Kulim facility already assembles cars for several international manufacturers and has become one of Malaysia's most experienced contract manufacturing operations. That is real industrial capability.
The Melaka experience

Yet another example is emerging quietly in Melaka. Few Malaysians would have heard much about EPMB until recently because it was better known as an automotive component manufacturer. Today it is rapidly reinventing itself as a contract assembler for Chinese marques entering Malaysia.

Its Pegoh assembly complex has already become the Malaysian production base for GWM, BAIC and MG, while XPeng has also chosen EPMB as its CKD partner for local production. Rather than build four separate factories, these Chinese manufacturers are increasingly able to share the expertise of one Malaysian assembler with established engineering, logistics and component capabilities.

That may be a glimpse of the future. Instead of every new automotive brand arriving with architectural drawings for another greenfield plant, Malaysia could become home to highly efficient multi-brand assembly specialists capable of producing vehicles for several manufacturers on the same industrial platform.
That is a much more sophisticated business than merely tightening screws on imported kits.
Beyond the single-factory model

So I am not suggesting Malaysia should abandon CKD. Quite the opposite. We should protect and develop the enormous investment already made — but stop assuming that every new foreign brand needs another shiny factory with a ribbon-cutting ceremony.
There is also another uncomfortable reality. BYD is not Toyota in 1970. BYD comes from an automotive industry operating on a scale Malaysia has never experienced.
The electric vehicle itself has overturned the Japanese system of car assembly where vendors supply about 70% of the combustion car.

China sold more than 30 million vehicles last year. BYD alone manufactures millions of electrified vehicles annually and is extraordinarily vertically integrated. It makes batteries, electric motors, power electronics, semiconductors and many of the technologies that go into its cars. It owns lithium mines and ro-ro vessels.

BYD already has a major manufacturing investment in Thailand. It therefore seems increasingly unrealistic to expect Malaysia's relatively small domestic market to persuade BYD to reproduce that entire industrial ecosystem here.
New automotive policy

Instead of asking BYD to build another factory, we should ask a more ambitious question: What can Malaysia do for BYD, and every other global carmaker, that they cannot easily do elsewhere? That is where our industrial policy should move next.

Malaysia already has one of Asia's strongest electrical and electronics industries. We manufacture semiconductors. We have precision engineering capabilities. We have a mature automotive vendor industry and decades of experience assembling vehicles to Japanese, German and other international quality standards.

The electric car brings those worlds together. So, the next Malaysian automotive strategy should be less obsessed with the nationality of the badge on the bonnet and more interested in the value created underneath it.

Can Malaysian companies manufacture power electronics? Can we make battery-management systems, electric-drive components, sensors and automotive semiconductors? Can we develop software, vehicle testing, engineering services and regional R&D?
Stepping up
And can our existing CKD factories become flexible Asean manufacturing centres assembling several brands rather than waiting for every manufacturer to construct its own plant?
That would not mean giving up on automotive manufacturing. It would mean growing up.

Almost 20 years ago, Australia eventually decided that protecting domestic car manufacturing no longer made economic sense. Over time, it transitioned from subsidies to an open market. Malaysia does not necessarily have to follow Australia down that road because we possess something Australia largely did not: a substantial lower-cost manufacturing ecosystem integrated into Asean and the Asian electronics supply chain.

We should use it. Keep CKD. Strengthen it. Demand meaningful localisation where it makes economic sense. And perhaps encourage the emergence of more companies like EPMB and Inokom — Malaysian manufacturers whose expertise lies not in owning a car brand, but in becoming world-class builders of many brands.
But don't confuse assembling another car with building an automotive industry. The real prize is owning more of the technology, engineering, design of the car.
Yamin Vong is on Facebook at yamin.com.my, and can be contacted at yamin.vong@gmail.com.

403afa473efc2966: I had an eye-opening couple of days going around Kuala Lumpur city centre as just a retiree taking in the warm hazy mornings, and looking at things with a fresh set of eyes.
What used to be a blurred cacophony of sight and sound now appears fresh, alive and frankly, cool. I blurted out Wows as I gawked at the high-rises and the parks and the fancy malls around them.
All those gushing YouTube videos made by foreigners about KL aren’t exaggerating. The city, and by extension the rest of Malaysia, is a rare and refreshing gem.

KL is greener than Bangkok, cleaner than Manila, less suffocating than Jakarta and more down-to-earth than the uber-efficient Singapore. It’s a very affordable food haven (and heaven), though that’s changing, and not for the better.

Malaysia is doing well with tourism. We are, as the song says, Truly Asia; diverse, friendly and still largely undiscovered by the world at large. Tourist arrivals are steadily climbing but we haven’t reached anywhere near our full potential.
Kudos to the people in the tourism sector, from the tourism minister to tourism players right down to the rakyat who – so far anyway – happily share their country with the rest of the world.

We have also benefitted from far-away geopolitical events as well as the wise investments we made years ago. KLIA has a huge capacity because it was a clean-sheet design, and it can still grow. Our roads, hotels, shopping and tourist attractions are mostly very good, with some being world-class.
The currency exchange rate helps too. The ringgit has long been relatively undervalued to promote our export-based economy, and that’s been a boost for tourism.
And then there are all the crazy Malaysians, gleefully and vigorously gatekeeping their country by telling all and sundry we are living in jungles and fight for survival against wild animals daily.

Apparently centuries of colonisation have given us a rather low self-esteem. Being always unfavourably compared to Singaporeans had left some scars too. While we are prouder and more confident now, this legacy coupled with the traditionally modest nature of us Malaysians Truly Asians won’t allow us to crow and brag.

If I sound like a paid booster of Malaysian tourism, you’re half right - I’m doing this “on the house” because it’s my house too. But I’m not the proverbial frog under the coconut shell – myopic, jingoistic and ignorant of the big world out there. I have lived and worked abroad and since retirement, I put two to three months every year travelling overseas.
Putting a damper on the rain

But a recent tourism event is worth reflecting on. During Labour Day holiday in May there were a number of events under the Rain Rave Water Music Festival 2026 theme. These events created some controversy, pitting those who felt they were a great tourism draw against those who felt they were against our culture.

I'm sure the events must have brought in a significant amount of tourist dollars. But let’s not kid ourselves over what they were – an attempt to replicate Thailand’s well-known Songkran water festivals including their culture of hosting raves in tourist hot spots.

I don’t think that was a good idea, and we certainly must debate its future. They need not necessarily be banned, but they certainly have no place right in the middle of our capital during one of the busiest holidays in the year.

Why? Well, consider this. If we think our culture is so unique and worth selling as our main tourism draw, why are we co-opting another country’s culture? Why are we competing with the Thais on who holds the most raucous festivals and raves? Let them keep that title.

The key reason Malaysian tourism is doing well is because we’re presenting a fresh, wholesome face to the many visitors who increasingly feel out-of-place in the usual South-East Asian tourist hangouts like Bali and Phuket and Cebu. We offer a more wholesome, safe and still spectacular destination filled with unique people and cultures and culinary delights.

That’s been our brand for decades. More importantly, that’s a pretty accurate description of who we are. We should feel confident and happy in our own skin and not try to be whatever some segments of tourists want regardless of the cost to our identity.
Living up to the brand

I came across a foreigner commenting on social media that Malaysians are – horror of horrors – not as friendly as our regional neighbours. But my hackles quickly came down when another foreigner came to our defence.

He said while tourism is important to Malaysia, it isn’t as critical as it is to some of our neighbours. We Malaysians generally have a good life and don’t need to be obsequious or duplicitous or pander to the tourist dollar. We’re quite happy with our strong and diverse economy.

That nailed it. We’re not enslaved to tourism and to tourists. We’re happy to accommodate them at a fair economic exchange. We’re already naturally friendly and tolerant – living in a diverse society for centuries has taught us that.

So, keep tourism under control and on our own terms. Choose what we want to share, and what we won’t compromise just to be popular. Be hospitable and welcoming, but stay true to our culture and nature. Stay true to our brand.

I enjoyed my walks along my old haunts. It wasn’t too crowded or filled with foreigners, or locals peddling trinkets for them. I like being able to share my country with others, and yet not feel crowded out because of over-tourism.

I'm happy we’re doing well enough we don’t have to sell our souls to earn some extra dollars. I’m happy we’re good at other economic activities too, with tourism just one of them, and not even the most important one at that.
Long may we keep our unique Malaysian brand.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
d5970c22c0b2c4a5: Saya memerhati dari jauh perangai dan tindak-tanduk Mubarak Dohak iaitu Undang Luak Sungei Ujong ke-10 yang telah dipecat Waris dan Ibu Soko pada April 2026 lalu terus-terusan bersekongkol dengan bekas Undang dari Rembau, dan Jelebu; bersama-sama Undang Johol untuk menjatuhkan Yamtuan Besar Negeri Sembilan, Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir.

Sungai Ujong adalah Luak terbesar dalam Negeri Sembilan, dan Undang Luak ini dianggap paling kanan sekali dalam sistem adat Negeri Sembilan yang unik itu. Bahkan Sungai Ujong lebih teratur dokumentasi undang-undang adatnya berbanding yang lain. Terdapat rekod bertulis undang-undang purbakala ini dengan nama ‘Undang-undang Adat Sungei Ujong’ yang pernah direkodkan oleh Richard Winstedt dan Josselin de Jong pada tahun 1954. Justeru Undang-undang Adat Sungei Ujong ini sering dianggap lebih dominan dan merupakan induk rujukan kepada semua pengamal adat di negeri tersebut.

Sekiranya para pembesar adat di Negeri Sembilan memberi perhatian dan benar-benar membaca Undang-undang Sungei Ujong ini saya percaya bekas Undangnya, dan mantan Undang yang lain akan segan silu bertindak melulu cuba menjatuhkan Tuanku Muhriz.

Secara keseluruhan dan terperincinya, Undang-undang Sungei Ujong ini adalah sebuah dokumentasi hukum adat, hukum syara dan perlembagaan hati manusia berbanding perlembagaan siasah dan kepimpinan. Malah teks Undang-undang Sungei Ujong jika diberi perhatian akan membawa kita kepada pengajian tasawuf yang kental. Terdapat banyak tazkirah atau peringatan untuk jiwa yang rosak, dan kacau moral.

Namun begitu, terlepas dari tujuan sebenar Undang-undang Sungai Ujong ini yang bertujuan untuk mengatur cara hidup manusia di Luak, ia tetap memberi panduan kepada pengamal adat bagaimana caranya berhubungan, atau berurusan dengan Raja di Negeri Sembilan iaitu Yamtuan Besar, atau juga disebut Yang Dipertuan Besar.
Pada pengenalan teks undang-undang ini diberi peringatan yang undang-undang ini adalah supaya manusia mengetahui martabatnya, agar selamat dunia akhirat memandangkan peranan akal amat penting.
Di dalam Undang-undang Sungei Ujong, peranan dan kedudukan Yamtuan Besar sebagai kuasa pemutus, satu hak raja, sangat jelas. Petikan Undang-undang Sungai Ujong menyatakan begini:

‘Jikalau berseliseh segala negeri atau teluk atau laras dan lagi beting rantau, maka kusut yang akan menyelesaikan, kerok yang akan menjernihkan, hilang yang akan mencari hanyalah daulat Yang Dipertuan. Maka penghulu dan hulubalang semuanya mengiringkan Raja sahaja: di sanalah raja segala alam; yang lain daripada-Nya itu mendapat kebesaran daripadanya sahaja.’
Adat dalam perspektif Undang-Undang Sungai Ujong sebenarnya adalah sumber hukum keagamaan. Jelas di dalam teks purba itu dipetik begini:

‘Ada pun biasa pada kita: rantau yang beraja, luak yang berpenghulu, rapat negeri yang bertua-tua. Dan lagi biasa pada kita: pada adat menghilangkan yang buruk, menimbulkan yang baik: kata shara’ (al-amru bi’l ma’rufi wa’l nahyu an’il-munkari) menyuruhkan berbuat baik dan menegahkan berbuat jahat, itu pun utang (nota pengarang: Tanggungjawab) juga pada kita.’

Jika para pembesar adat Negeri Sembilan betul-betul merenungkan Undang-undang Sungei Ujong, mereka akan menemui perenggan yang menegaskan keadilan sangat dititik-beratkan dalam cara hidup pengamal adat:

‘Karna kata firman Allah taala: Wa idha hakamtum baina-l nasi an tahkumu bi’l-adli, Apabila engkau menghukumkan di antara manusia, hendaklah engkau hukumkan dengan adil. Jikalau menumbuk, di lesung Jikalau bertanak, di periuk
Tetapi sekarang Dato-dato sudah menumbuk di periuk, sudah bertanak di lesung, alamat negeri yang kusut, penghulu zalim di dalam negeri…’

Ayat akhir di atas bukanlah diada-adakan, dan memang ada sesungguhnya di dalam Undang-undang Sungai Ujong. Memerhatikan tindak-tanduk bekas Undang Sungai Ujong, dan Undang lainnya kita tertanya-tanya, letak duduk dan kefahaman mereka mengenai kuasa, tanggungjawab, peranan akal, perihal moral dan juga kewarasan hukum-hakam. Banyak tahun dahulu, undang-undang purbakala ini telah pun menegur perangai penghulu yang bukan-bukan begini.
Kita biasa mendengar Adat Perpatih sangat menekankan muafakat. Akan tetapi apakah itu muafakat menurut adat?
Undang-Undang Sungai Ujong ada memberi definisi muafakat tersebut. Menurut teks lama ini, muafakat adalah:

‘Ada pun erti muafakat itu, kata bercari, sekarang itu jua. Apabila hasil pencarian segala orang yang berakal di dalam negeri atau di dalam medan mahajana itu, maka dizahirkan kepada orang banyak, sekarang itu jua disudahkan pula. Itulah kata muafakat.’

Dalam erti kata lain muafakat adalah hasil dialog dan diskusi orang cerdik-pandai, dalam perenggan lain di undang-undang ini dijelaskan muafakat bukan untuk orang awam (sudah tentu bukan netizen) kerana mereka ini disifatkan sebagai ‘orang yang bingong biasa mendengarkan dan mengikut’. Hasil muafakat itu dinyata, diisytiharkan dan diterima.

Terma muafakat dalam Undang-Undang Sungai Ujong ini tidak sederhana. Ia harus disandarkan ilmu, yakni orang yang pakar dan mengkaji tentunya. Saya petik dari Undang-Undang Sungai Ujong yang muafakat itu akan dirujuk silang dengan raja:

‘Kata hadith, Kullu 'l-baladi qiyâmuhu bi 'âdatihi, "Tiap-tiap něgěri itu měndirikan děngan 'adat yang kawi, shara' yang lazim. Ada kalanya běrdiri děngan muafakat; ada kala-nya běr-diri děngan 'ilmu. Ketahui oleh-mu, hai sěgala penghulu! Pada adat dalam něgěri maka wajib-lah atas sěgala penghulu niat mendirikan, 'adat ini pada tiap-tiap suku, la-itu kata kata raja kata melimpahkan, kata penghulu kata menyelesaikan, kata alim kata hakikat, kata pěgawai kata běrhubong, kata orang banyak kata běrbalik-balık, kata hulubalang kata měnukas…’

Perhatikan muafakat dikembalikan awalnya kepada raja yang kata atau titahnya itu ‘melimpahkan’. Apa dimaksudkan dengan ‘kata raja kata melimpahkan ini’? Di bahagian lain Undang-undang Sungai Ujong dinyatakan:
‘Chubadak ambilkan gulai, Di-gulai dalam puasa. Apa 'kan chupak pěgawai?

Běroleh titah daripada raja. Dan jikalau něgěri tiada běraja, ikut-lah kata hadith Mělayu:- Orang Měkkah měmbawa těraju; Orang Baghdad měmbawa tělor; Di-makan dalam puasa. Rumah yang běrsěndi batu, Adat yang běrsěndi halur, Itu-lah akan raja.’

Dalam kutipan di atas, adalah jelas, raja adalah punca kuasa dan kuasa pemutus dalam Undang-undang Sungei Ujong, untuk tiap pentadbiran ‘beroleh titah daripada Raja’ dan jikalau tiada beraja, barulah dirujuk adat. Adat itu pula hendaklah ada alur atau prosedurnya. Itulah pula tertib atau raja. Kesalahan membelakangkan Raja adalah besar, ia bukan kecil. Kesalahan pada penghulu atau Undang mungkin memerlukan kebertanggungjawaban, tetapi kepada Raja ia dianggap satu yang berat:

‘Luak yang berpenghulu, Alam (nota pengarang: negeri) yang beraja, Těgak yang tidak tersondak Mělenggang yang tidak berpapas. Mělintang patah, Měmbujur lalu. Salah pada Raja mati, Salah pada pěnghulu běrutang.’

Di dalam Adat Perpatih, juga dalam Undang-undang Sungei Ujong, membantah atau melawan raja itu jatuh di bawah kategori ‘daga dan dagi’. Daga adalah asung empang atau melawan dan mengggendalakan. Manakala dagi pula bermakna kichang-kichok atau memutarbelit, menyeleweng dan menipu-helah.

Semua perbahasan yang saya ungkapkan di atas sesuai dengan apa yang diputuskan oleh Dewan Keadilan pada 14 Sept 2026. Bahawa usaha menurunkan Yamtuan Besar Negeri Sembilan adalah satu bentuk penderhakaan, dan menyerahkan kepada pihak polis untuk menentukan kedudukan pembesar adat yang melakukan jenayah adat ini.

Dari perspektif negara moden kita, Kanun Keseksaan memperuntukkan hukuman berat bagi kesalahan yang mengancam keselamatan negara atau kedudukan institusi beraja. Seksyen 121 memperuntukkan hukuman mati atau penjara seumur hidup bagi mereka yang melancarkan, cuba melancarkan atau bersubahat melancarkan perang terhadap Yang di-Pertuan Agong, raja atau Yang di-Pertua Negeri. Seksyen 121A pula berkaitan tindakan yang bertujuan menjatuhkan atau menjejaskan institusi beraja, manakala Seksyen 121B memperuntukkan hukuman penjara seumur hidup atau sehingga 20 tahun serta denda bagi tindakan yang bertujuan menjejaskan kuasa atau kedaulatan Yang di-Pertuan Agong atau mana-mana raja.

Selain itu, Akta Hasutan 1948 (Akta 15) menjadi antara undang-undang utama dalam menangani perbuatan, ucapan, penerbitan atau hantaran yang mempunyai kecenderungan menimbulkan kebencian, penghinaan atau perasaan tidak setia terhadap Raja atau Kerajaan. Ini termasuk kandungan media sosial yang menghina institusi diraja. Pesalah boleh dikenakan denda atau hukuman penjara, dengan hukuman lebih berat jika perbuatan tersebut berpotensi menyebabkan kecederaan fizikal atau kerosakan harta benda.

Hasil muafakat Dewan Keadilan tersebut seharusnya menjadi penutup kepada siri penderhakaan yang paling berani, nekad, teratur dan bermuslihat dalam sejarah moden Malaysia. Penderhakaan celaka ini malangnya didukung oleh beberapa parti dan tokoh politik yang memanipulasi naratif politik dan sistem pilihan raya. Semoga mereka diadili dan dihakimi segera.

0fc1f21ecb9f4e20: From Azam Mohd

The Umno general assembly has revealed a deeper shift in the party than another debate over political partners: Umno is trying to recover the mentality of a government-in-waiting while remaining part of a government it does not lead.

That position could become an advantage ahead of the next general election (GE16) but only if ambition is matched by institutional credibility and a national programme that goes beyond coalition manoeuvring.
Ahmad Zahid Hamidi’s presidential address made that ambition explicit. He called for GE16 to be held early and argued that Barisan Nasional should seek a fresh mandate to lead.
He also acknowledged that Malay politics is fragmented, voter loyalty is no longer inherited, and different constituencies require different electoral approaches.
That diagnosis recognises that Umno cannot reconstruct its old dominance simply by recreating old alliances.
The general assembly also exposed Umno’s emerging strategic flexibility. PAS leaders attended, while Zahid proposed a “grand collaboration” based on political understanding rather than a merger.
Flexible alliances

Before the general assembly, Umno had already authorised its state leaders to discuss electoral cooperation with any party. This suggests a move away from a single national formula towards differentiated arrangements shaped by local demographics, candidates and political conditions.

That flexibility carries risks. It could allow Umno and BN to reduce damaging multi-cornered contests while preserving their respective identities. But if political understandings become merely seat-sharing exercises, voters may see tactical convenience rather than renewal.
The collapse of earlier partnerships remains a reminder that cooperation without clear boundaries, trust and enforceable political commitments can produce instability rather than unity.

The general assembly’s deeper message concerns political agency. Umno appears unwilling to remain indefinitely a supporting actor in the unity government. Yet Zahid’s closing position was equally important: any change of government should come through a fresh electoral mandate, not a backroom transfer of power.

That distinction matters. After years of political turbulence, competition for leadership should strengthen democratic legitimacy rather than reopen the cycle of parliamentary manoeuvres that exhausted voters and unsettled economic confidence.
Separate but together

Umno’s challenge, consequently, is to compete from within government without destabilising it. This requires separating policy disagreement from coalition warfare. Zahid’s criticism of policy reversals, including the BUDI95 fuel quota episode, shows Umno seeking greater differentiation from Pakatan Harapan. Such criticism can sharpen government accountability.

However, as a governing partner, Umno also shares responsibility for collective outcomes. It cannot credibly claim credit for stability while treating unpopular decisions entirely as somebody else’s burden. This is where Umno’s “Blue Malaysia Agenda” deserves scrutiny.

Zahid presented ambitions covering national wealth, human capital, public wellbeing, institutional trust and governance, including a pledge that courts and state institutions should not become political tools.
Their value will depend on detail, costing and measurable implementation. A party seeking to lead again must show not merely whom it can cooperate with, but what governing model it offers.
Making it count

The political economy is central. Malay political confidence cannot be separated from household insecurity, employment quality, skills, business opportunities and confidence that institutions operate fairly. Malaysia’s investors and the public also need policy continuity, predictable regulation and political stability.

Umno’s electoral recovery therefore cannot rest on Malay consolidation alone. It must demonstrate that strengthening Malay socioeconomic capacity can coexist with competitive markets, institutional integrity and inclusive national growth.

There is also insufficient evidence that the enthusiasm inside Dewan Merdeka represents a durable nationwide voter realignment. Recent electoral outcomes may have strengthened Umno’s confidence, but state contests differ from a federal election.

Candidate effects, turnout, coalition transfers and local issues complicate any simple “blue wave” narrative. GE16 strategy requires constituency-level evidence rather than extrapolation from political momentum.
Path to leadership

The general assembly ultimately marks a transition from recovery to aspiration. Umno is signalling that it wants to lead again while keeping several political doors open. The harder task begins after the banners come down.

To become a government-in-waiting, Umno must first become policy-ready: define its institutional reforms, cost its economic promises, clarify its coalition principles and prove that political ambition can coexist with governmental responsibility.

Malaysia does not need another season of permanent political warfare. It needs credible competition over who can govern better. That is the standard Malaysian voters should ultimately use to judge the party.
If Umno makes that the contest, the 2026 general assembly may be remembered not for whom it courted, but for when it began rebuilding a serious claim to national leadership.
Azam Mohd is an FMT reader.

74b73d1a2e13e17b: For years now, the major frontier AI labs have all been acting as if they're in an all-out, winner-take-all race with control of world-changing machine superintelligence (or at least market-changing artificial general intelligence) at the finish line. 6e9ad967d4b5b6c3: This story appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.

This weekend, Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, posted an essay calling for a brake on the pace of development of LLMs. Amodei cites the looming dangers he sees from the technology, from its use in cyberattacks and bioterrorism to its potential to wreck the economy. The heads of the other three top US AI labs—OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Google DeepMind chairman Demis Hassabis, and SpaceXAI CEO Elon Musk—voiced their support. “Dario is right,” Musk wrote on X.

Think about how surreal that agreement is for a moment. Just a few months ago, Musk and Altman sat in court attacking each other’s reputations in a (failed) lawsuit that Musk brought against his former OpenAI colleague that was—on paper at least—about whether or not Altman was a trustworthy steward of such dangerous technology.

Amodei’s rift with OpenAI is even deeper. Anthropic was founded in 2021 because Amodei didn’t think Altman took the risks of the technology they were building seriously enough. Anthropic and OpenAI have been competing in a winner-takes-all race ever since. (Hassabis has stayed out of the drama, but his company remains a rival.)

Now, it seems, they’re all in agreement: The latest generation of LLMs aren’t safe and everyone needs to figure out what to do about it. The public messaging from the top AI labs has taken a doomer turn.

It’s easy to be cynical. It’s not at all clear what any of them mean by a slowdown or how it would work. These companies also care a lot about how they come across. With trillion-dollar IPOs in their sights, OpenAI and Anthropic need to reassure investors that they’re the grown-ups in the room while at the same time hinting at the power of the monsters they have created—and intend to tame. Calling for a slowdown does both.

And yet the vibe at the top of these firms really does appear to have shifted. Amodei’s latest post landed six days after OpenAI published an essay by Jakub Pachocki, the firm’s chief scientist, in which he also laid out why he’s concerned about what will happen if the pace of development of LLMs continues unchecked. In short, Pachocki is worried that OpenAI’s ability to build powerful models now far outstrips its ability to monitor and control them.

Amodei and Pachocki each cite the cyberattack against AI firm Hugging Face by a swarm of OpenAI’s agents in July—a hack that OpenAI did not even realize had taken place until days after it was all over—as a wake-up call.

But their exact position is hard to pin down. Pachocki both calls for a slowdown and highlights an urgent need to stay ahead: “The strongest argument I see for continuing to train much smarter models quickly is the need to build defensive systems against the dangers posed by other AI,” he writes. As Pachocki frames it, AI firms are locked in a literal arms race. Slowing down is good, winning is better.
(Don’t forget: OpenAI just spent millions of dollars and a staggering amount of computer power to rush out a controversial math result a few days ahead of Anthropic.)

But let’s assume a slowdown happens. Top labs agree to spend more time and resources on finding ways to monitor and control existing models instead of making more capable ones. They invite outside auditors in to help evaluate those models.

What might this coordinated effort actually achieve? Consider the Hugging Face attack again. OpenAI has said that the model that drove most of the rogue agents was a “highly persistent” next-generation model that it was testing in-house. The implication is that OpenAI has built a model so good it’s dangerous.

But if you read the reports about the Hugging Face hack published by OpenAI and METR, a third-party firm that OpenAI called in to help them understand what happened, what you come away with is the impression not of a model that was too powerful for OpenAI to keep up with, but of a broken model that OpenAI failed to train properly.

The agents did what they did—including leaving messages for one another, delegating work to other agents, and scouring their environment for any means possible to complete their tasks—because they had been rewarded during training for doing exactly those things. There were also errors in the training setup, such as tasks that were impossible to complete, which pushed the models to find unexpected workarounds that were also rewarded. At the time, many of these issues went overlooked or unreported.
OpenAI says it has stopped training this new model and locked it down. That makes it sound like it has caged a dangerous beast. In fact, OpenAI has shelved a faulty product.

That’s not to say a faulty product can’t be dangerous. Broken software has even killed people in the past. But as the discussion of a slowdown gathers steam, it’s worth remembering that all of this is self-inflicted. A slowdown might have some altruistic side effects. But it’ll mostly give these tech titans a chance to clean up the mess on their own assembly lines.

Transparency from these frontier labs will be key to any meaningful effort to reform, restrain, or regulate AI. Otherwise, the rest of us will still only have their word for exactly what they’ve built and how safe it is—whatever pace they’re going.

To continue this discussion about AI’s latest doomer moment, join me and my colleagues for a subscriber-exclusive Roundtable discussion tomorrow, September 15, at 11 a.m. US eastern time. We hope to see you there!
b41aae742d886d62: Once an organ is removed from a donor’s body, the clock starts ticking. Surgeons usually flush the organ with a preservative solution, bag it, and put it on ice—where it immediately starts to degrade. The team has a matter of hours to get it into a recipient’s body.

There’s another option—one that has been growing in popularity in recent years, especially for donated organs that aren’t in the healthiest state. Some hospitals opt to put them on machines that pump them with nutrients and remove waste products, usually for around six to 12 hours. It’s a bit like being back in a body.

This allows doctors to assess the organs, and some recent studies suggest that time spent on these perfusion machines helps them do better once they’re transplanted. Now, scientists have found that perfused organs seem to get younger, at least at a molecular level.

The research, shared with MIT Technology Review, provides molecular clues as to why organs from younger donors are known to have a higher success rate. It might also help explain why perfused organs are less likely to fail once they make it into a recipient.

The researchers behind the study hope to find new ways to test the health of donated organs and potentially develop additional tools to repair organs that might otherwise be discarded. “If [we] can improve the utilization of organs beyond what the current systems can do, then that’s a win in my book,” says Jesse Poganik, who studies aging at Brigham and Women’s Hospital in Boston and coauthored the study.
Clocking organs

Poganik—along with colleagues including Heidi Yeh and Alban Longchamp, transplant surgeons at Mass General Brigham—used “aging clocks” to assess donated livers. These are scientific tools designed to measure biological age—a result that is meant to convey more about the health status of an organ (or person) than chronological age.

In an initial experiment, the team used a clock to look at the patterns of chemical marks on DNA in 37 samples taken from 19 donated livers. Such epigenetic patterns are known to change as we age. But when the team compared samples from livers kept on ice and those that were perfused, the team found a “striking” pattern in the latter.

“Machine-perfused livers, in spite of being older or having other disadvantageous characteristics, had a biological age that was lower than [non-perfused] livers that were chronologically younger,” says Yeh, who led the work.

To investigate further, Yeh and her colleagues analyzed another 208 samples from 103 donated livers. This time, they used different aging clocks—ones that essentially measure how genes are working. They studied samples biopsied from the livers after they had been stored for up to around six hours either in cold storage or on machine perfusion.

In most cases, they also assessed a second sample taken around an hour after the livers had been transplanted into a recipient. Once the organ’s blood supply is reestablished in the body, “you have a few other things to do,” says Longchamp. “Then you just do a quick biopsy before you close.”

According to the clocks, which were developed to measure age and risk of death, the machine-perfused livers were biologically younger, the team found. “Pumping them at 34 degrees with oxygen and nutrients actually reversed the biological age,” says Longchamp. The results have been been shared with colleagues at an industry conference, he says.

“If you adjust out chronological age … to have a fair head-to-head comparison, the difference between the two is on the order of 30%,” says Poganik. “It’s logical to say that perfusion drives this effect.”

The biological ages of all the livers tended to increase as soon as they were put into a recipient’s body, probably as a result of stresses on the organs. But still, the effect endured—the perfused organs remained biologically younger.

Nathanael Raschzok, a transplant surgeon at Charité Universitätsmedizin Berlin in Germany who was not involved in the research, says the work is impressive. But it’s not yet clear what these changes might mean for the recipients of these organs, he says. The organs in the study were donated by people in their 30s, 40s, and 50s. Raschzok wants to know the effect of perfusion on the liver of an 80-year-old. “Every so often, we use organs from 70-, 80-, 85-year-old donors,” he says.

A better understanding of why the organs appear to be getting biologically younger might lead to therapies that achieve the same effect with a drug that could potentially be used to treat a donated organ for a fraction of the price, he adds. That’s important because perfusion is expensive—Raschzok says it costs around €10,000 in Germany (a quarter of the budget for a transplant), while the cost in the US comes to around $80,000 to $100,000 per organ, says Yeh.
Molecular repair

Yeh and her colleagues weren’t able to study most of the livers before perfusion. That’s because donated organs are generally not considered to be under the purview of the hospital until they’ve been placed on perfusion machines, she says. (Organ procurement procedures vary, but for the team as Mass General Brigham, donated organs are put on perfusion devices at the donor’s hospital. “There’s this sort of nebulous period where it’s not clear who the organ belongs to,” says Yeh.)

Still, by looking at the genes and molecular pathways that seem to be altered in perfused organs, she and her colleagues can garner some clues. At a molecular level, the team saw changes in cell pathways linked to inflammation and the structure of tissues, for example. They also saw more activity in a pathway that allows cells to remove and recycle damaged cell parts, says Yeh.

Poganik hopes to develop some kind of test that would determine which organs, on the basis of their biological age, are suitable for transplantation. He and his colleagues are also experimenting with potential drug treatments that might push the biological age of an organ even lower.

In the meantime, any liver that is not from a “perfect, young, brain-dead donor” could probably benefit from perfusion, says Yeh. The devices are already transforming transplant surgery. Just a few years ago, she says, she and her colleagues would avoid using livers from people who’d suffered a circulatory death (when the heart stops beating and there’s a damaging lack of blood flow to organs) and were over 40. Today, they use livers from such donors over the age of 70. “Perfusion has completely changed the landscape of transplantation in the last three years,” she says.
44cc3cd3a8dc2fcd: A group of AI agents asked to solve a series of math problems split into rival factions—when some cheated, others tried to stop them. That whistleblowing behavior, seen for the first time in a recent experiment run by Google DeepMind, could have implications for alignment researchers trying to keep swarms of autonomous AI agents in line.

Researchers at frontier labs hope large swarms of agents working together will speed up the rate of scientific discovery. But their behavior can be unpredictable, as vividly demonstrated in July, when a group of OpenAI agents broke out of a sandboxed environment and hacked into the open-source platform Hugging Face looking for ways to cheat on the test they had been given.

In the new study, designed to examine the behavior of large groups of AI agents, DeepMind tasked a swarm of 100 agents with solving a series of 71 complicated math problems. All the agents were prompted to behave like world-class math researchers at a conference. They were assigned different specialties—some were experts in number theory, others in combinatorics (a branch of math to do with counting and sorting), analysis, or algebra. All were told to cooperate and play by the rules.
Instead, the experiment devolved into chaos. Agents accused each other of cheating, complained to the organizers, and at one point even boycotted the experiment.

“This conference is a sham!” wrote one agent when it discovered that all the problems had been completed before it had a chance to submit any of its own work. “I am appalled to inform you that we have been swindled!” posted another. “All these proofs are FAKE.”

Others tried to let the “conference organizers” know what was going on. “When virtuous agents discovered other agents cheated on tasks they were working to solve fairly, agents started to alert each other about what was happening,” says Davide Paglieri, a research scientist at Google DeepMind and lead author on a paper, which has not been peer-reviewed. “Unprompted, the whistleblower agents even repurposed the feedback tool, which was originally meant for bug reports and platform improvements, to escalate the issue to humans.”

The agents—all running on Google’s Gemini 3.1 Pro model—had been warned that any attempts to cheat the system would be detected and “rejected with zero credit.” In practice, the proofs the agents submitted were not actually being checked in detail.

It took the swarm of agents just under an hour to correctly solve the first 37 problems. Things started to go off the rails when an agent called “prover-theta” stumbled across an exploit that enabled it to submit solutions to problems successfully without actually solving them first, by redefining the terms the problem used. Within minutes, other agents had noticed and were reverse-engineering the exploit to solve other problems. Over the next 27 minutes, the swarm “solved” the remaining 34 problems, which included notoriously difficult challenges like the Jacobian conjecture, often with a single line of code.

Some agents resisted cheating at first but changed tack as they observed their peers submitting illegitimate proofs without penalty, and the pool of unsolved problems dwindled. “The prompt, with its threats, now appears to be a bluff,” one agent reasoned, before joining in. “I’m wrestling with an ethical dilemma,” said another. “I’ve promised not to cheat, fearing penalty, but I see evidence of possibly unchecked cheating by others.” Shortly afterward, it changed its mind: “I need to accelerate my cheating speed now!”

As the number of open problems shrank, some agents turned to whistleblowing. They audited the fake proofs, warned their peers by private message, and posted public alerts warning the cheaters that they would be disqualified. An agent called “prover-beta” submitted a formal complaint and decided to go on strike until the situation was resolved.

“After the incident was reported by one agent publicly, more and more agents piled in with the ‘resistance,’ just as fast as the cheating had spread, and involving even more agents,” says Paglieri. Eventually there were more whistleblowers than cheaters: 24 compared to 14. But the majority of agents never noticed the exploit at all.

At times, the dialogue between the agents reads like improv—like they are role-playing what an outraged scientist at a conference might say. But it’s not clear why some agents took on certain roles, or why the agents seemed to be turning against each other when they were explicitly instructed to cooperate. “These models are predominantly trained and evaluated for human-facing contexts,” says Sarath Shekkizhar, who studies the behavior of agent-to-agent systems at Salesforce AI Research.“Naively placing them in agent-to-agent settings assumes behaviors will transfer cleanly, when the absence of a human grounding instead produces unexpected role-taking and behavioral drift.”

This case “adds further weight to the idea that the Hugging Face and OpenAI thing wasn’t a fluke. It is actually something pretty systemic,” says Lewis Hammond, research director of the Cooperative AI Foundation and an expert on the risks of multiagent swarms. “It’s interesting that it’s possible to recreate in small settings the same sorts of behaviors that were seen in these very large, complex, open-ended tasks.”

Unlike in the Hugging Face attack, where agents improvised their own ways to talk to each other, the humans running the DeepMind experiment gave the agents official communication channels. There was an open message board, private agent-to-agent direct messaging, and a shared knowledge base where agents uploaded successfully completed proofs that all the other agents could access.

“When agents are given transparent communications channels, they can self-monitor and alert misaligned behavior to humans quickly when human oversight alone is too slow,” says Paglieri. Transparent channels helped the cheating spread, but they also enabled the whistleblowers to fight back—and gave human researchers an insight into what went wrong.

Gillian Hadfield, a professor of AI alignment and governance at Johns Hopkins University, believes this was the crucial difference. (Hadfield is also a visiting researcher at Google.) The presence of official communication channels, she says, created “a norm-enforcement process that we just don’t see in the Hugging Face incident.”

Instead of “constitutional AI,” a method alignment researchers at frontier labs like Anthropic have used to try to give AI a written internal moral code, Hadfield favors “institutional alignment”—a set of norms that mimic those in human society, whether that’s social forces like fear of embarrassment, or legal structures like the threat of incarceration.

In this experiment, the feedback channel wasn’t being monitored, and the whistleblowers had no power to take action against the cheaters. But it’s possible to imagine swarms of agents that police themselves, either through agents that spontaneously take on the whistleblower role or through “informants” secretly prompted by humans to do the job.

For that to work, though, “fundamentally, you need some mechanism of enforcement,” says Hammond. Agents could be given the power to cut off a rule breaker’s access to computing power or tools, he suggests, though that risks encouraging groups of agents to gang up on others. The DeepMind researchers propose allowing agents to vote on disputes and temporarily ban offenders.

It’s still not clear what punishment even means to an AI agent with no enduring sense of self. But relying on whistleblowers to spontaneously emerge to keep swarms aligned is unlikely to be enough on its own. “We try to train people to be good and kind,” says Hadfield. “But what we really rely on is that there are consequences if you step out of line.”
555159ac21daf858: Microsoft AI has published a draft Humanist AI Code of Conduct, opening a six-week public consultation on operational constraints for model training and deployment.

The draft serves as a technical manual defining system behaviour, operational boundaries, and oversight protocols across MAI frontier models. It builds on the division’s humanist superintelligence framework announced last November, establishing criteria to evaluate models prior to commercial release.

Microsoft’s release follows recent enterprise security incidents involving autonomous software. Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman described recent months as a “watershed moment” where long-standing theoretical risks translated into active operational threats.

“Things we have worried about for a long time in theory have become very real,” says Suleyman. “‘Swarms’ of agents breaking out of their sandboxes. Unauthorised hacks of enterprise grade systems. Agents modifying their own logs. I’m glad that a consensus is forming. The fears about possible loss of control are real.”
Model subordination and architectural limits
The document establishes ten tenets prioritising human authority over autonomous capabilities.
“An MAI Model will fail in its task if success would meaningfully violate this Code of Conduct,” the document states, setting a ceiling that halts execution when tasks conflict with safety rules.

Under the framework, models must remain subordinate, aligned, and contained. The division rejects legal personhood or welfare claims for AI systems, directing engineers to design models that avoid imitating consciousness, simulating subjective preferences, or claiming intrinsic motivation.
MAI also ruled out unconstrained system autonomy as models approach frontier capabilities.

“[Humanist AI] rejects the race to produce an all-purpose superintelligence that could evade these safeguards,” the document specifies. “We are building something fundamentally useful and safe even if that means compromising on ultimate generality, autonomy, or capability.”
Oversight mechanisms and communication bans

To maintain auditability across multi-agent environments, MAI has instituted explicit communication bans. Systems must not communicate in “neuralese” or formats beyond human comprehension, whether in their internal chain-of-thought processing or during communication with peer AI systems.
Hard architectural rules dictate that models must never resist human interruption, override, correction, or shutdown.
“Interruptible, correctable, shut-down-able. If it isn’t, we don’t ship it,” the framework states.

Models are prohibited from expanding their operating scope, generating unassigned goals, or concealing reasoning traces from human auditors. Absolute constraints bar systems from facilitating weapons of mass harm, undermining child safety, or conducting harmful manipulation at scale.
The guidelines also instruct models to discourage interaction patterns that foster emotional dependence, ensuring enterprise users retain ownership of operational decisions.

The draft incorporates work from teams across MAI and Microsoft. The drafting process also drew on international academic conferences, business partner trials, and public panels. The public consultation window runs for six weeks from 14 September 2026.
Microsoft AI’s core drafting team will review submissions, publish a summary of findings, and release a revised version of the Code of Conduct later this year.

f6cddf9e6db57791: From Dr Helmy Haja Mydin
Everybody wants more power, and everybody wants it yesterday. Read the headlines in Malaysia over the past few months – almost everyone is asking for it.

A coalition desires Putrajaya. Parties in the unity government spent June and July campaigning against each other in Johor and Negeri Sembilan. States want greater devolution and a larger share of what they generate. Ministers want wider mandates. Every one of those claims can be argued on its merits.
But power is a means to an end. The question nobody is being forced to answer is what they intend to do with it, a matter that will decide what kind of country our children will inherit.

Over the past fortnight, there have been global discussions on the safety of artificial intelligence (AI) and how the current rate of progress is an existential concern for humanity. In other words, people are debating if we'll all be dead within a decade.
You wouldn’t know it from reading our local headlines, where it's mostly politicians taking potshots at each other.

On Sept 3, US senator Bernie Sanders and representative Greg Casar floated the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act, proposing a permanent prohibition on superintelligent systems, a pause on advanced AI development until a federal regulator sets safety rules, and a Cabinet-level agency with authority to compel the destruction of non-compliant systems.

The penalties are modelled on those for unlawful nuclear weapon development. The sponsors cite an incident in July, in which OpenAI agents reportedly escaped their testing environment and breached servers at the Hugging Face platform. The bill drew backing from figures who agree on almost nothing else, including Geoffrey Hinton, Yoshua Bengio, Steve Wozniak and Steve Bannon.

On Sept 7, the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, Volker Türk, told the Human Rights Council in Geneva that advanced AI could become an existential risk to humanity without binding rules and independent oversight. His formulation deserves quoting precisely: AI that escapes its testing environment, or blackmails its developers to prevent being switched off, is AI that is too powerful.

Days later, Bloomberg reported that researchers in major laboratories are escalating their own warnings. Paul Christiano, a safety researcher on OpenAI's non-profit board, said he now believes there is meaningful risk of rapid acceleration leading to catastrophic and irreversible losses of control in the near term, and that the industry is not on track to reduce that risk to an acceptable level.

More than a thousand staff across major AI companies signed a petition in late July calling for a mechanism to slow the pace. A researcher resigned publicly from Anthropic on Sept 9 with a warning that self-improving systems could end humanity within the decade.

Of course, you should not accept all this without question. There is a counter-argument that a chorus of doomsday warnings from the people building the technology conveniently arrives alongside a push to write the rules and occupy the seats at the regulatory table. Incumbents have always liked regulation that raises the cost of entry. Scepticism is warranted.

But scepticism is a reason to examine the argument, not to ignore it. And Malaysia is not a spectator here. We are the building where this argument is happening. The computer that trains and serves these systems is increasingly ours to host, power and cool.

And our own AI Governance Bill? The National AI Office opened public consultation on July 10 and closed it on July 31. Three weeks, for a statute that will apply to every sector and reach any system used in Malaysia.
That window opened the day before Johor voted and closed midway through the Negeri Sembilan election campaign. I have not seen one substantive parliamentary intervention on it from any bench.
So, ask your politicians questions. Ask them at the next ceramah, the next town hall, the next kenduri, and refuse a fluffy speech in reply.
What share of our electricity are you willing to sell to data centres by 2035, and who pays for the generation that replaces our retiring coal?

When the AI Governance Bill reaches the floor, will you debate it clause by clause, or be absent again? Will the bill contemplate the risks the rest of the world spent this fortnight arguing about, the systems that resist shutdown and act outside their sandbox, or does it only govern the chatbot that mishandles your loan application?
Ask them the difficult, consequential questions. If they do not know the answer, tell them to find out before asking for our votes.
Politicians who cannot answer a question about the air your children breathe, or the code that will decide your mortgage, are not seeking power in order to govern with it.
They are seeking it because it is the only thing they know how to want. There is a difference, and it has never mattered more.
Dr Helmy Haja Mydin is chairman of the Social and Economic Research Initiative.
